header: Mst. Rukhsana Habib Vs. The State and others
Muhammad Nauman Vs. The State and others
Muhammad Zeeshan Vs. The State and others
body: Date of hearing: 22.10.2026 Mr. Sajjad Hussain Qureshi, Advocate, for the Petitioner in Writ Petition No. 11427/2026.

Ms. Rubina Magassi, Advocate, for the Petitioner in Writ Petition No. 11728/2026. Sardar Mehboob, Advocate, for the Petitioner in Writ Petition No. 11013/2026. Malik Masroor Haider Usman, Additional Advocate General and Mr. Sittar Sahil, Assistant Advocate General, with Shahid/SI, Tariq/SI and Asma/SI. Ms. Naheed Kanwal, Deputy District Public Prosecutor.
Ms. Muneeza Manzoor Butt, Senior Psychologist, Violence Against Women Centre, Multan.
Barrister Khadija Yasmin Bokhari, amicus curiae.

Ms. Amna Khan, Advocate, for Respondent No.4 in Writ Petition No.11013/2026. Tariq Saleem Sheikh, J. – These three constitutional petitions, Writ Petition Nos.11427/2026, 11728/2026 and 11013/2026, arise from orders whereby the Judicial Magistrate recorded the statements of two girls, Mafia Bibi and Saleena Bibi, under section 164 Cr.P.C. and then directed that they be lodged in Dar-ul-Aman, Multan. As the petitions raise common questions of law, I am considering them together through this order. The facts of each case are set out below.

Writ Petition No.11427/2026 2. The Petitioner is the mother of Mafia Bibi. On 31.08.2026, she got FIR No.862/2026 registered under section 365-B PPC at Police Station Basti Malook, Multan, against unknown persons, alleging that her daughter had left home on 23.08.2026 and had not returned. During the investigation, Mafia Bibi appeared before the Judicial Magistrate, Section-30, Multan, to have her statement recorded under section 164 Cr.P.C. On 07.09.2026, upon receiving notice, the Petitioner appeared before the Magistrate and produced Mafia Bibi’s Form-B, according to which she was born on 21.12.2009 and was sixteen years, eight months and seventeen days old on that date. Mafia Bibi, however, stated that she had contracted marriage with Muhammad Nauman of her own free will and wished to reside with him. Relying upon Form-B, the Magistrate held her to be a minor within the meaning of the Punjab Child Marriage Restraint Act, 2026 (the “2026 Act”), and directed that she be lodged in Dar-ul-Aman, Multan, “till further orders of the competent court or till she attains lawful age.” The Petitioner claims that her daughter subsequently contacted her through Dar-ul-Aman’s official telephone number and expressed a desire to accompany her. She, therefore, applied for Mafia Bibi’s release, but the Magistrate dismissed her application by order dated 15.09.2026, reiterating the reasons for the original placement. The Petitioner states that she thereafter approached the Additional Sessions Judge, Multan, by way of criminal revision, but the Court did not entertain it on the ground of maintainability. She has not impugned that order but has challenged the order dated 15.09.2026 before this Court in its constitutional jurisdiction.

Writ Petition No.11728/2026 3. This petition also relates to Mafia Bibi, whose mother has filed Writ Petition No.11427/2026, supra. Petitioner Muhammad Nauman claims that Mafia Bibi contracted marriage with him on 18.08.2026 of her own free will, against the wishes of her parents. He alleges that her parents subsequently lodged a false FIR against him. He maintains that Mafia Bibi was approximately eighteen years old at the time of marriage and that the Form-B produced before the Magistrate was fabricated to show her as a minor. He further states that, in her statement recorded under section 164 Cr.P.C. on 07.09.2026, Mafia Bibi affirmed that she had contracted marriage with him voluntarily and without coercion. She also expressed apprehension of danger to her life from her parents and wished to reside with Nauman. Nevertheless, the Magistrate directed that she be lodged in Dar-ul-Aman by order dated 07.09.2026, referred to above. Nauman further claims that Mafia Bibi subsequently contacted him through Dar-ul-Aman’s official telephone number and expressed her desire to accompany him. He therefore applied for her release, but the Magistrate dismissed his application by order dated 11.09.2026, reiterating the grounds for her placement in Dar-ul-Aman. The instant petition challenges that order.

Writ Petition No.11013/2026 4. In this petition, Muhammad Zeeshan asserts that Saleena Bibi, whom he describes as approximately nineteen years old, contracted marriage with him on 25.07.2026 of her own free will, against the wishes of her parents. Her father subsequently lodged FIR No.758/2026 dated 04.08.2026 under section 365-B PPC at Police Station Shah Jamal, Muzaffargarh. Meanwhile, Saleena Bibi approached the Judicial Magistrate, Section 30, Multan, for recording her statement under section 164 Cr.P.C. The Magistrate summoned the relevant record and issued notice to her parents. On 03.09.2026, she recorded Saleena Bibi’s statement, in which the latter stated that she had contracted marriage voluntarily and wished to reside with Muhammad Zeeshan. Her father produced a Form-B showing that she was fourteen years, eleven months and nineteen days old. Relying upon that document, the Magistrate held her to be a minor. She further held that her consent carried no legal value and directed that she be lodged in Dar-ul-Aman until further orders of the competent court or until she attained the lawful age. Zeeshan challenged the order dated 03.09.2026 through a criminal revision before the Additional Sessions Judge, Multan, who held, by order dated 10.09.2026, that the direction for placement in Dar-ul-Aman was ancillary to the proceedings under section 164 Cr.P.C. and was not amenable to revision. He accordingly disposed of the revision as not maintainable, leaving the Petitioner to seek relief before the High Court. Muhammad Zeeshan has challenged both orders through this petition.

The submissions 5. Mr. Sajjad Hussain Qureshi, counsel for the Petitioner in Writ Petition No.11427/2026, contended that the Magistrate had no lawful authority to direct Mafia Bibi’s placement in Dar-ul-Aman while recording her statement under section 164 Cr.P.C., much less for an indefinite period. He submitted that the Magistrate dismissed the Petitioner’s application for her release without ascertaining Mafia Bibi’s wishes or considering the claim for parental custody. Referring to her NADRA Form-B, which recorded her date of birth as 21.12.2009, counsel maintained that she was a minor and that her alleged marriage with Muhammad Nauman attracted the 2026 Act. He argued that sections 5 and 13 of the Act precluded treating the alleged marriage or Mafia Bibi’s consent as sufficient grounds for entrusting her custody to Nauman. He also disputed the genuineness of the Nikahnama. He accordingly prayed that the Magistrate’s orders dated 07.09.2026 and 15.09.2026 be set aside and Mafia Bibi be released to her mother’s custody.

6. Ms. Rubina Magassi, counsel for Muhammad Nauman in Writ Petition No.11728/2026, also questioned the Magistrate’s authority to commit Mafia Bibi to Dar-ul-Aman. She submitted that Mafia Bibi was sui juris and had contracted marriage with Nauman of her own free will. She disputed the authenticity of the Form-B produced by her parents and maintained that the 2026 Act was not attracted. Alternatively, she argued that any contravention of the Act did not invalidate the marriage. According to counsel, Nauman, being the lawful husband, was entitled to Mafia Bibi’s custody. She further submitted that the Magistrate failed to give due consideration to Mafia Bibi’s statement under section 164 Cr.P.C. and dismissed Nauman’s application for her release without ascertaining her wishes afresh. Counsel argued that Mafia Bibi could not lawfully be confined in Dar-ul-Aman against her will and sought her release to accompany Nauman. She relied upon Nasim Khalid v. The State (NLR 1988 Criminal 546) in support of her submissions.

7. Sardar Mehboob, counsel for Muhammad Zeeshan in Writ Petition No.11013/2026, challenged the Magistrate’s order dated 03.09.2026 directing Saleena Bibi’s placement in Dar-ul-Aman and the subsequent order dated 10.09.2026 whereby the Additional Sessions Judge declined to entertain the criminal revision. He submitted that Saleena Bibi had voluntarily contracted marriage with Zeeshan and had expressly stated before the Magistrate that she wished to reside with him. He disputed the conclusion regarding her minority, maintaining that she was approximately nineteen years old. Counsel contended that section 164 Cr.P.C. did not empower the Magistrate to determine Saleena Bibi’s custody or direct her compulsory residence in Dar-ul-Aman. He further questioned the Additional Sessions Judge’s conclusion that the placement order, being ancillary to the recording of her statement, was not amenable to revision. He prayed that both orders be set aside and Saleena Bibi be released.

8. Malik Masroor Haider Usman, Additional Advocate General, submitted that the 2026 Act merely criminalises the solemnization of child marriages without affecting their validity. According to him, a marriage voluntarily contracted by a girl who has attained puberty is valid under Islamic law. Referring to section 21 of the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 (the “GWA”), he contended that the husband is the lawful guardian of his minor wife and is entitled to her custody unless found unfit to act as her guardian. Her voluntary residence with him cannot, therefore, be regarded as illegal custody. He further submitted that a minor cannot be compelled to reside with her father or remain in a shelter home against her wishes unless the competent Guardian Court has determined the question of custody. As regards jurisdiction under the 2026 Act, he argued that section 8 empowers the Court of Sessions to take cognizance of and try offences under the Act and to exercise the powers contemplated therein. He maintained that where such a matter comes before a Magistrate, it may be referred to the Court of Sessions under section 190 Cr.P.C. In support of his submissions, he relied upon Shahbaz Masih v. Additional Sessions Judge, Lahore (PLD 2026 FCC 138), Mushtaq Ahmad v. Mirza Muhammad Amin (PLD 1962 (W.P.) Karachi 442) and Muhammad Mustafa v. District Police Officer (2026 LHC 3118).

9. Ms. Naheed Kanwal, Deputy District Public Prosecutor, referred to the Islamic concepts of bulugh and rushd and Verse 6 of Surah An-Nisa to submit that physical maturity and intellectual discretion were relevant to assess a girl’s capacity to make an informed decision concerning marriage and residence. She argued that where a girl aged sixteen or seventeen years had voluntarily contracted marriage and expressed a clear preference to accompany her husband, her wishes deserved consideration notwithstanding her minority. She referred to section 17(3) of the GWA in support of this submission and added that continued confinement in Dar-ul-Aman against the girl’s wishes could itself be detrimental to her welfare.

10. Considering the importance of the issues involved, this Court, by order dated 24.09.2026, issued notice to Ms. Muneeza Manzoor Butt, Senior Psychologist, Violence Against Women Centre, Multan, and former District Women Protection Officer, and appointed Barrister Khadija Yasmin Bokhari as amicus curiae for assistance. Both filed written submissions, which have been examined.

11. Ms. Muneeza Manzoor Butt submitted that, under Islamic law, a girl who has attained puberty and voluntarily contracted Nikah enters into a valid marriage, which is not dissolved or invalidated merely because protective measures are taken. She maintained that where a minor faces competing parental and matrimonial claims, the Court must exercise its parens patriae jurisdiction, keeping in view her safety, dignity, and bodily integrity under Articles 9 and 14 of the Constitution. According to her, compelling a minor to return to a parental home where she apprehends coercion or retaliatory harm could endanger her safety and psychological well-being. Equally, prolonged residence in Dar-ul-Aman against her wishes could cause emotional distress. In her opinion, permitting a minor to accompany the person claiming to be her husband, subject to appropriate safeguards, might present a lesser immediate risk than compulsory restoration to parental custody.

12. As regards protective arrangements, Ms. Butt recommended that any permission for a minor to accompany the person claiming to be her husband should be subject to appropriate safeguards. These might include a surety bond furnished by him and his family, an undertaking concerning the minor’s education, counselling to defer pregnancy until she attains eighteen years, and supervision by the District Women Protection Officer through unannounced visits and monthly reports. She also proposed a restraining order against the minor’s family to prevent harassment, threats or unlawful interference. Referring to the Punjab Protection of Women against Violence Act, 2016 (the “Women Protection Act”), and the Punjab Women Protection Authority Act, 2017, she submitted that the statutory protection system could help safeguard the minor’s education, health, and psychological well-being. She acknowledged that, under section 13 of the 2026 Act, the child’s wishes were relevant but not conclusive, and that any protective arrangement required an independent assessment of her safety and welfare, including the possibility of coercion or undue influence.

13. Barrister Khadija Yasmin Bokhari, amicus curiae, disagreed with Ms. Butt’s recommendation for conditional release to the person claiming to be the husband. She submitted that section 5 of the 2026 Act treats cohabitation resulting from child marriage as child abuse, irrespective of consent, and that no undertaking, surety or monitoring arrangement could authorise conduct prohibited by statute. According to her, the validity of the alleged marriage did not determine the child’s entitlement to protection or justify her delivery to the adult contracting party. Referring to section 13, she argued that the child’s wishes remained relevant but were not conclusive, and that the Court must independently assess her safety and welfare. She also cautioned against automatic restoration to parental custody, particularly where allegations of coercion or retaliatory harm required examination. In her submission, the appropriate arrangement should follow an assessment of the risks associated with the available alternatives.

14. On the question of jurisdiction, the amicus curiae submitted that a Magistrate recording a statement under section 164 Cr.P.C. could make a limited interim arrangement for the custody of a child requiring protection. She invoked the doctrine of parens patriae and the protective scheme of the 2026 Act in support of that jurisdiction, while acknowledging that permanent guardianship and custody fell within the competence of the appropriate court. She further maintained that the availability of other remedies did not exclude this Court’s constitutional jurisdiction to examine the legality of continued institutional custody. As regards the appropriate accommodation, she favoured the Child Protection and Welfare Bureau over prolonged residence in Dar-ul-Aman and proposed that any such arrangement follow an independent assessment and remain subject to judicial review. She also suggested guidelines for determining age, ascertaining the child’s wishes and assessing the suitability of the proposed placement.
15. I have heard counsel for the parties and considered the assistance rendered by the amicus curiae and Ms. Muneeza Manzoor Butt. The following questions arise for determination:
(i) Whether a Judicial Magistrate recording a statement under section 164 Cr.P.C. may direct that the person making it be kept in Dar-ul-Aman.
(ii) What consequences the 2026 Act attaches to a child marriage in relation to cohabitation, residence and custody, and what weight the child’s wishes carry.
(iii) What protective jurisdiction the Court of Sessions possesses under the 2026 Act, and how it relates to the jurisdiction of the Guardian Court and the protective mechanisms of other enactments.
(iv) Whether the impugned orders are sustainable in law and what relief, including any immediate protective measures, is warranted in the circumstances of these cases.

Child Marriage: The Earlier Law 16. Under Islamic law, marriage (Nikah) is a civil contract founded upon the consent of the contracting parties. The consent must be voluntary and free from coercion. The capacity to contract marriage has traditionally been associated with the attainment of puberty (bulugh), which, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, is presumed upon attaining fifteen years of age. Islamic jurisprudence, however, distinguishes physical maturity (bulugh) from intellectual maturity (rushd), which bears upon a person’s ability to understand the nature and responsibilities of marriage. In Pakistan, statutory law also regulates matrimonial capacity and restrains child marriage.

17. The Child Marriage Restraint Act, 1929 (the “1929 Act”), was enacted to restrain the solemnization of child marriages. As applicable in Punjab before its repeal, it defined a child as a male below eighteen years or a female below sixteen years of age and prescribed punishment for an adult male contracting a child marriage and for persons solemnizing, promoting or permitting such a marriage. It did not, however, expressly declare a marriage contracted in contravention of its provisions void or voidable. The Majority Act, 1875, also distinguishes the general age of majority from the capacity to contract marriage. While section 3 prescribes eighteen years as the general age of majority, section 2 excludes from its operation the capacity of any person to act in matters of marriage, dower, divorce and adoption. Consequently, the age of majority under that Act did not determine matrimonial capacity, while the 1929 Act imposed penal restrictions upon child marriage without expressly determining its civil validity.

18. In Mst. Bakhshi v. Bashir Ahmad (PLD 1970 SC 323), the question arose whether a marriage contracted with a minor in contravention of the 1929 Act was invalid. The case concerned a Muslim girl who had attained the age of fifteen years but was below sixteen. The Supreme Court held that she was presumed to have attained puberty under Islamic law and that her marriage was valid notwithstanding the statutory prohibition. It explained that although the 1929 Act prohibited the marriage of a girl below sixteen years, “the marriage itself does not become invalid on that score”, while the adult husband and persons responsible for solemnizing it could incur criminal liability. The Court thus distinguished the penal consequences of child marriage from its civil validity. Other decisions followed the same distinction.

In Allah Nawaz v. Station House Officer (PLD 2013 Lahore 243), this Court also recognised it. That decision preceded the 2026 Act and cannot be applied to disregard the prohibition in section 5. Its further holding that section 375(v) PPC did not apply where the girl acknowledged the marriage is debatable. However, that question Mushtaq Ahmad v. Mirza Muhammad Amin (PLD 1962 (W.P.) Karachi 442); Mauj Ali v. Syed Safdar Hussain Shah (1970 SCMR 437); Ghulam Hussain v. Nawaz Ali (1975 PCrLJ 1049); Zafar Khan v. Muhammad Ashraf Bhatti (PLD 1975 Lahore 234); and Allah Bakhsh v. Safdar (2006 YLR 2936). need not be examined, as it does not arise for determination in these petitions.

19. In Farooq Omar Bhoja v. Federation of Pakistan (PLD 2022 FSC 1), the Federal Shariat Court (FSC) examined the restrictions imposed by sections 4, 5 and 6 of the 1929 Act and held that the State could restrict an otherwise permissible (mubah) act to prevent harm to society or any segment thereof. Applying the principle of Sad-uz-Zaraey, it held that the impugned restrictions were not repugnant to the Injunctions of Islam. In Ali Azhar v. Province of Sindh (PLD 2023 FSC 265), the FSC considered whether prescribing eighteen years as the minimum marriage age for both sexes under the Sindh Child Marriages Restraint Act, 2013, was repugnant to the Injunctions of Islam. Referring to Verse 6 of Surah An-Nisa, the Court held that marriage “does not depend only on the fact that either the parties to a marriage have attained the age of puberty or not, but it requires certain mental maturity also, which is commonly called as Rushd.”

It further held that a minimum age “provides [a] reasonable time period [for] girls to complete basic education at least, which normally helps in developing mental maturity (Rushd)”, and that fixing such an age “is not against the injunctions of Islam”.

These decisions affirm the Legislature’s authority to prescribe a minimum marriage age notwithstanding the traditional relevance of puberty. They also answer the DDPP’s submission regarding the capacity of girls aged sixteen or seventeen, although the weight of a child’s preference regarding residence remains a separate question. Neither decision determines the civil validity of a marriage contracted in contravention of child-marriage legislation.

20. In Mst. Mumtaz Bibi v. Qasim (PLD 2022 Islamabad 228), the Islamabad High Court took a different view of the consequences of child marriage. Referring to sections 375 and 377-A PPC, section 23 of the Contract Act, 1872, and the statutory framework for the protection of children, it concluded that a marriage involving a person below eighteen years was a contract entered into for an unlawful purpose and was, Ali Azhar v. Province of Sindh (PLD 2023 FSC 265), para. 6. ibid., paras. 9 and 11.

therefore, void ab initio. The Court observed that “A marriage contract in which one of the parties is a child under the age of 18” was a contract executed for an unlawful purpose. With respect, insofar as this reasoning treats the criminal prohibition of child marriage as necessarily rendering the marriage void, it cannot be reconciled with the distinction drawn by the Supreme Court in Mst. Bakhshi between the penal consequences of a marriage and its civil validity. Section 2 of the Majority Act preserves the law governing matrimonial capacity, while the 1929 Act did not expressly prescribe nullity as a consequence of its contravention. To that extent, the reasoning in Mumtaz Bibi does not correctly state the law. The judgment nevertheless makes a valid distinction between the attainment of puberty and the capacity to make a free and informed decision concerning marriage. That distinction is relevant to the assessment of consent.

21. In Muhammad Riaz v. District and Sessions Judge, Islamabad (2026 CLC 381), the Islamabad High Court reconsidered the question under the Islamabad Capital Territory Child Marriage Restraint Act, 2025. It expressly disagreed with Mumtaz Bibi, holding that the statutory prohibition of child marriage and the punishment prescribed for its contravention did not, in the absence of an express provision, necessarily render the marriage void. This conclusion accords with Mst. Bakhshi. The Court also permitted a girl below eighteen years of age to reside with the person claiming to be her husband, without examining section 5 of the Islamabad Act, which treats cohabitation resulting from child marriage as child abuse irrespective of consent.

22. The Federal Constitutional Court subsequently considered the earlier statutory framework in Shahbaz Masih v. Additional Sessions Judge, Lahore (PLD 2026 FCC 138), decided on 03.02.2026. The case concerned the alleged marriage of a girl whose father disputed her age, conversion to Islam and matrimonial status. Referring to the 1929 Act and the earlier Supreme Court decisions, the Court observed that the legislation “merely criminalizes the solemnization of a child marriage” without expressly declaring the marriage void or voidable. It also upheld the refusal to recover the girl from the person claiming to be her husband, having regard to the circumstances examined in that case. The judgment was rendered under the earlier statutory framework. The alleged marriages in the present petitions took place after the commencement of the 2026 Act, which expressly prohibits cohabitation resulting from child marriage and prescribes additional safeguards under section 13. The consequences of the alleged marriages for residence and custody must, therefore, be examined under the new legislation.

Matrimonial Status and Custody 23. The validity of a marriage does not determine entitlement to the custody of a minor. In proceedings under section 491 Cr.P.C., the legality of detention must be distinguished from the enforcement of matrimonial rights. In Muhammad Rafique v. Muhammad Ghafoor (PLD 1972 SC 6), the Supreme Court considered a case in which the High Court directed an adult woman to be delivered to the person claiming to be her husband against her wishes. The Supreme Court set aside that direction, holding that even a decree for restitution of conjugal rights could not be enforced by compelling a wife to accompany her husband.

The Court, however, distinguished the position of a minor, observing that “if the person is a minor, the Court may make over his custody to the guardian which will be dealing with him in accordance with law”. This observation did not determine which claimant was entitled to the minor’s custody or dispense with the requirements of the applicable guardianship law.

24. In Allah Dad v. Hazur Bakhsh (1985 SCMR 942), the Supreme Court considered the custody of a girl whose age, according to the relevant birth record, was approximately fourteen years, although medical opinion placed her between sixteen and seventeen. She claimed to have married the petitioner and expressed her desire to accompany him. The Lahore High Court preferred the documentary evidence concerning her age and found that her expressed wishes could not safely be regarded as voluntary, particularly because she had remained under the petitioner’s influence. The Supreme Court upheld the order restoring her custody to her father, subject to a contrary determination by a competent court. The decision illustrates that an alleged marriage and a child’s expressed Mst. Sahi Bi v. Khalid Hussain (1973 SCMR 577).
preference are not conclusive where the circumstances cast doubt on her age, voluntariness or welfare.

25. In Shahida Parveen v. Muhammad Inayat (PLD 1980 Lahore 14), a girl whose age and alleged marriage were disputed had been placed in Dar-ul-Aman following the recording of her statement under section 164 Cr.P.C. The Sessions Judge subsequently directed that her custody be entrusted to her father. Upholding that order, the Lahore High Court observed that she “cannot be kept there for the entire period of litigation or trial of the case which may ultimately even go to appeal.” It further considered that her delivery to the person claiming to be her husband would be inappropriate while the alleged marriage and his involvement in her abduction remained in controversy. The decision is significant in two respects. It holds that continued residence in Dar-ul-Aman cannot ordinarily serve as an indefinite substitute for a lawful determination of custody, and that an alleged matrimonial relationship does not entitle the person asserting it to obtain custody of a minor.

26. The position of the husband as guardian of a married minor female was considered in Mushtaq Ahmad v. Mirza Muhammad Amin and another (PLD 1962 (W.P.) Karachi 442). A Division Bench of the erstwhile High Court of West Pakistan observed that, under the GWA, the Court could not appoint a guardian of the person of a married minor female unless it considered her husband unfit. The Court recognised the validity of the marriage under the law then applicable and directed the girl’s release from her father’s unlawful custody, leaving her free to accompany her husband. In Sajjad Hussain v. Superintendent, Dar-ul-Aman, Multan and others (1990 PCr.LJ 791), a learned Single Judge of this Court distinguished the attainment of puberty from majority for guardianship purposes. Referring to Mushtaq Ahmad, the Court considered the husband’s claim to custody upon proof of marriage, but declined to act upon the alleged marriage because its existence had not been established. These decisions demonstrate the legal significance of the matrimonial relationship under the earlier law. They do not, however, dispense with the determination of a disputed custodial claim under the applicable legislation. The Punjab Child Marriage Restraint Act, 2026 27. The Punjab Child Marriage Restraint Act, 2026 (Act XXVII of 2026), which came into force on 11 May 2026, repealed the 1929 Act and the Punjab Child Marriage Restraint Ordinance, 2026, subject to the saving contained in section 15(2), and introduced a substantially different legal regime. Section 2(c) defines a “child” as a person, male or female, below eighteen years of age, while section 2(d) defines “child marriage” as an act of Nikah or solemnization of marriage where either or both contracting parties are children. The Act thus adopts a uniform age threshold. Section 3 prohibits the registration of child marriages, and section 4 makes an adult contracting marriage with a child liable to punishment.
28. The 2026 Act goes further than the earlier legislation and treats cohabitation resulting from a child marriage as child abuse, irrespective of the child’s consent. Section 5 provides:

5. Child abuse and its punishment. – (1) Any form of cohabitation, before attaining the age of eighteen years, with or without consent, resulting from a child marriage shall be the child abuse under the Act.

(2) Any person who induces, forces, persuades, entices or coerces any child bride or child groom to engage in child abuse or commits child abuse shall be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years but shall not be less than five years and with fine which shall not be less than one million rupees.

29. The term “cohabitation” is not defined in the 2026 Act. Black’s Law Dictionary defines it as “the fact or state of living together, esp. as partners in life, usu., with the suggestion of sexual relations.” In its ordinary meaning, therefore, cohabitation denotes living together in a relationship of a domestic or matrimonial character. Read in the context of section 5(1), the expression “any form of cohabitation” extends to such living arrangements resulting from a child marriage and is not confined to sexual intercourse. The child’s consent is immaterial, but liability under section 5 requires proof of the conduct constituting cohabitation. Section 5 does not, however, expressly declare the marriage void or voidable. The Black’s Law Dictionary, 9th Edn., p.296.
prohibition of cohabitation must, therefore, be distinguished from the question of matrimonial validity.

Protective Powers under the 2026 Act 30. The 2026 Act confers specific powers upon the Court of Sessions for the protection of children affected by child marriage. Section 2(g) defines the “Court” as the Court of Sessions as provided under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898. Section 8 provides that, notwithstanding section 190 Cr.P.C., no court other than the Court of Sessions shall take cognizance of or try an offence under the Act. Section 9 separately empowers that Court to issue an injunction where it is satisfied, upon an application, that a child marriage is about to be arranged. Section 12 makes the provisions of the Code applicable, mutatis mutandis, subject to the Act. The AAG submitted that a Magistrate could refer proceedings under the Act to the Court of Sessions under section 190 Cr.P.C. This submission is misconceived. Section 8 excludes the Magistrate’s jurisdiction to take cognizance of or try offences under the Act. Section 190 Cr.P.C. does not authorise him to entertain or refer an application for protective custody. In the present cases, no proceedings under the 2026 Act were before the Magistrate.

31. Section 13, entitled “Best interests of the child”, gives substantive content to the Court’s protective responsibilities. Subsection (1) provides that “[i]n all actions and decisions taken under this Act, including prevention, investigation, prosecution, bail, sentencing and protective injunctions, the best interests of the child shall be a primary consideration.” Subsection (2) requires consideration of the child’s safety, physical and mental health, education, development and views, having regard to age and evolving capacities. It also expressly includes “immediate protective needs, including safe shelter and supervised custody where required”. Subsection (3) provides that no child shall be treated as an offender merely by reason of being a contracting party to a child marriage. Subsections (4) to (7) of section 13 address situations in which a child’s removal from lawful guardianship and alleged marriage give rise to competing claims regarding residence or custody. Subsection (4) provides that, in proceedings under the Act, where a child has been taken, enticed, induced, coerced, trafficked or otherwise removed from lawful guardianship for the purpose of marriage, the Court shall not treat the child’s statement or purported consent to accompany the adult contracting party as determinative of custody, residence or protective orders. Subsection (5) requires an independent and reasoned assessment of the child’s safety, welfare and best interests, having regard to the circumstances of removal, coercion or undue influence, age and vulnerability, the likelihood of further harm and the necessity of protective custody or safe shelter. Subsection (6) makes it clear that voluntary consent alone does not defeat the Court’s protective jurisdiction, while subsection (7) requires priority to be given to the child’s safety, dignity, education and long-term development over claims founded upon marital status, customary practice or alleged consent. The child’s wishes remain relevant, but their weight must be determined in the light of these statutory considerations.

32. Section 13 must, however, be read in the context of the 2026 Act as a whole. Although it contemplates protective custody and safe shelter, it does not confer a general jurisdiction to determine custody or exercise the powers ordinarily vested in a Guardian Court. Subsection (1) refers to actions and decisions taken “under this Act”, subsection (4) to “proceedings under this Act” and subsection (5) to “cases under this Act”. Subsection (1) extends the best-interests requirement to actions and decisions at various stages, including prevention and investigation, but does not independently confer jurisdiction upon the Court of Sessions. The requirement applies to authorities lawfully exercising their respective powers. Similarly, the reference to the Court’s “protective jurisdiction” in subsection (6) must be understood in relation to powers otherwise available under the Act, including the injunction under section 9.

Interaction with Other Protective Laws 33. The Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, read with the Family Courts Act, 1964, governs the adjudication of guardianship and custody. Section 7 empowers the Court to appoint or declare a guardian where the minor’s welfare so requires. Section 12 authorises interim orders for the production and protection of a minor, while section 17 prescribes the considerations governing appointment or declaration of a guardian. Section 12(3)(a), however, expressly prohibits the Court from placing a female minor in the temporary custody of a person claiming guardianship on the ground of being her husband, unless she is already in his custody with the consent of her parents, if any. Section 19(a) precludes the Court from appointing or declaring a guardian of the person of “a minor who is a married female and whose husband is not, in the opinion of the Court, unfit to be guardian of her person.” Section 25 deals with the return of a ward who has left or been removed from the custody of a guardian, subject to the Court being satisfied that such return would serve the ward’s welfare.

34. The AAG’s contention that a husband is entitled to the custody of his minor wife by virtue of section 21 of the GWA proceeds upon a misreading of that provision. It concerns a minor’s capacity to act as guardian, not an adult husband’s rights. Section 19(a), on the other hand, recognises the husband’s position under the applicable personal law, but its effect is confined to restricting the appointment or declaration of another guardian where he is not considered unfit. It does not dispense with the separate question whether custody should be entrusted to him. That distinction is reinforced by section 12(3)(a), which expressly restricts temporary custody in favour of a person claiming guardianship as husband. Moreover, section 19(a) cannot be read in isolation from section 5 of the 2026 Act, which prohibits cohabitation resulting from child marriage before the age of eighteen. That prohibition must be respected in determining any proposed custodial arrangement, but does not conclusively determine the husband’s fitness for guardianship. The DDPP’s reliance upon section 17(3) is also subject to the welfare requirement outlined in subsection (1). The minor’s intelligent preference deserves consideration, but cannot override a statutory prohibition or determine custody independently of her welfare.

35. Under section 5 of the Family Courts Act, read with its Schedule, the Family Court exercises exclusive jurisdiction over custody of children and guardianship. Section 25 of that Act deems the Family Court to be a District Court for the purposes of the Guardians and Wards Act. Appointment or declaration of guardianship and the determination of custody are distinct matters, although both fall within the Family Court’s jurisdiction. The jurisdiction thus conferred extends to adjudicating competing custodial claims and making appropriate interim arrangements. The child’s alleged marriage does not determine the outcome of such proceedings.

36. The Punjab Destitute and Neglected Children Act, 2004 (the “Children Act”), prescribes a separate procedure for the protection of children falling within its statutory definition of a destitute and neglected child. However, section 4(1) restricts the initiation of proceedings under Part VII to children who have not attained fifteen years of age, though the proceedings already initiated may continue after that age. Section 24 permits a Child Protection Officer to take such a child into custody and requires production before the competent Court within twenty-four hours, subject to the safeguards prescribed therein. Section 25 provides for temporary custody in a child protection institution pending such production, and section 26 for the production of a child who is in the custody of a parent or guardian. Section 27 expressly requires the Court to examine on oath the person producing or reporting the child and provides for the recording of evidence during the inquiry. Under section 28, the Court may order admission to a child protection institution or entrust custody to a suitable person where the statutory conditions are satisfied. The Act thus expressly regulates both the circumstances justifying protective intervention and the procedure for determining the child’s custody under Part VII. The Children Act may also apply to a child affected by marriage under the 2026 Act, but a child marriage does not, by itself, attract its provisions. The statutory conditions for intervention must be independently satisfied.

37. The Women Protection Act provides another protective mechanism. Its provisions may also apply to a girl involved in a child marriage where she has been subjected to violence within the meaning of section 2(1)(r) of that Act. Under sections 4 and 6 to 8, the Family Court may entertain a complaint and issue interim protection or residence orders, including relocation to a shelter home where the statutory requirements are fulfilled. The Act also provides for Women Protection Officers and shelter facilities to assist persons requiring protection. The provisions governing rescue and assistance expressly recognise the woman’s consent. Section 15(1) provides that a Women Protection Officer “shall not rescue the aggrieved person without her consent”, while section 16(3) excludes assistance where the woman “has voluntarily refused to accept such assistance”.
The availability of a shelter facility or other protective assistance does not confer authority to order compulsory custody outside the applicable statutory provisions.
Magistrate’s Authority under Section 164 Cr.P.C.

38. Section 164 Cr.P.C. empowers a Magistrate of the First Class, or a Magistrate of the Second Class specially empowered in that behalf, to record statements and confessions during investigation or before the commencement of an inquiry or trial. The provision prescribes the manner of recording such statements but does not confer jurisdiction to determine custody. A statement so recorded does not constitute a judicial determination of the facts stated by its maker or of her entitlement to reside with a particular person. Its evidentiary use in criminal proceedings must be distinguished from the consideration of the maker’s expressed wishes in an inquiry into her protection or custody.

39. In Muhammad Ashiq v. Superintendent of Dar-ul-Aman (1973 PCr.LJ 79), the Magistrate ordered the detention of an alleged abductee in Dar-ul-Aman for six months after recording her statement under section 164 Cr.P.C., although she claimed to be legally married and wished to accompany her husband. The Lahore High Court found that she was competent to contract marriage under the law then applicable and was not an accused person but, at most, a prosecution witness. The Court observed that “there is no law, which authorised the Magistrate to send her to Darul Aman and be detained there, especially, when she claimed to be major and wanted to accompany her husband.” The detention order was consequently set aside. Although the decision turned on her capacity to marry, it supports the distinction between recording a statement under Sections 15(1) and 16(3) of the Punjab Protection of Women against Violence Act, 2016. section 164 Cr.P.C. and exercising an independent power to order detention.

40. In Nasim Khalid v. The State (NLR 1988 Criminal 546), a Magistrate directed that a woman recovered under section 100 Cr.P.C. be kept in Dar-ul-Aman against her wishes. The Lahore High Court held that her detention was unlawful and ordered her release, observing that a Magistrate, District Magistrate or Sessions Judge had no lawful authority to send unwilling women or girls, whether major or minor, to Dar-ul-Aman. The case concerned a woman who was sui juris. The wider observation regarding minors cannot exclude protective custody expressly authorised by a particular enactment. The decision nevertheless reinforces the principle that compulsory placement in Dar-ul-Aman requires lawful authority.

41. The position is not altered merely because the person appearing before the Magistrate is a child within the meaning of the 2026 Act. The amicus curiae submitted that the doctrine of parens patriae, read with the protective scheme of that Act, empowered the Magistrate to make an interim arrangement for her custody. The submission cannot be accepted because neither section 164 Cr.P.C. nor that doctrine independently confers such jurisdiction upon the Magistrate. This does not preclude the Magistrate from exercising any protective power conferred upon him by another enactment. Where the circumstances disclose the commission of an offence under the 2026 Act, the Investigating Officer should proceed in accordance with the prescribed procedure. If the child also requires immediate protection, the Investigating Officer may approach the court or authority competent under the applicable law to make the necessary arrangement.

The Present Cases 42. Applying the foregoing principles, the orders directing Mafia Bibi and Saleena Bibi to remain in Dar-ul-Aman cannot be sustained. Both girls appeared before the Judicial Magistrate for recording their statements under section 164 Cr.P.C. Relying on their respective Forms-B, she held them to be minors and directed that they remain in Dar-ul-Aman until further orders of the competent court or until they attained the lawful age. These directions restricted their liberty for an indefinite period without any assessment of the necessity of such custody or provision for its review. Section 164 Cr.P.C. did not authorise the Magistrate to make those orders, and she identified no other source of jurisdiction. The subsequent orders declining Mafia Bibi’s release suffer from the same defect.

43. In Saleena Bibi’s case, the Additional Sessions Judge declined to entertain the revision, holding that the Magistrate’s direction was ancillary to the recording of her statement under section 164 Cr.P.C. This reasoning overlooks the fact that the direction restricted her personal liberty and required an independent legal basis. Even if the revision was not maintainable, the Additional Sessions Judge could have examined whether relief was available under section 491(1A) Cr.P.C. Its description as a revision did not preclude consideration of that remedy. The availability of such a remedy does not exclude this Court’s jurisdiction under Article 199(1)(b)(i) of the Constitution to examine the legality of the girls’ custody.

44. In Muhammad Mustafa v. District Police Officer (2026 LHC 3118), relied upon by the AAG, a learned Single Judge of this Court directed the release of a girl above fifteen years of age from Dar-ul- Aman. She wished to reside with her maternal aunt. The case did not involve child marriage or any statutory prohibition affecting her proposed residence. It is, therefore, distinguishable.

45. In Muhammad Aslam v. Additional Sessions Judge (2026 LHC 5390), another learned Single Judge declined to permit a girl below eighteen years of age to accompany the person with whom she had contracted marriage after the commencement of the 2026 Act. That conclusion accords with section 5 of the Act. The learned Judge also directed that the girl be entrusted to the Child Protection and Welfare Bureau. She had already attained fifteen years of age, whereas section 4(1) of the Children Act restricts the initiation of proceedings under Part VII to children below that age. The question of statutory authority for that direction was neither raised nor decided. The judgment is, therefore, not authority upon that question.

46. According to the Forms-B produced before the Magistrate, both Mafia Bibi and Saleena Bibi are below eighteen years of age. Muhammad Nauman disputes the authenticity of Mafia Bibi’s Form-B, while Saleena Bibi claims to be nineteen years old. The official records have not so far been displaced, and the Investigating Officers have also reported that both girls are minors. Although both girls have expressed a wish to accompany the persons claiming to be their husbands, neither that wish nor their minority alone determines the competing claims to custody. Their safety and welfare require an independent assessment.

47. Ms. Muneeza Manzoor Butt has drawn attention to the psychological effects of prolonged residence in Dar-ul-Aman and the risks which may arise from compelling a girl to return to a family opposed to her marriage. Her observations do not establish that either girl’s parents are unfit, but they indicate the need to examine the safety of such an arrangement. Her recommendation for conditional release to the alleged husbands cannot be accepted because residence with them would amount to cohabitation prohibited by section 5. The available record does not permit a satisfactory assessment of the girls’ circumstances or of the suitability of other arrangements.

48. The question remains what relief should be granted in these petitions. As explained above, section 13 of the 2026 Act prescribes the considerations governing decisions in proceedings under the Act but does not independently confer jurisdiction to determine custody, whether temporary or permanent. No proceedings under that Act are presently pending before the Court of Sessions. Both girls have attained fifteen years of age, and no proceedings under Part VII of the Children Act were initiated before they reached that age. Section 4(1) of the Children Act, therefore, precludes the initiation of such proceedings now. The disputed questions concerning their ages, safety and suitable accommodation cannot be satisfactorily resolved on the available record without further inquiry. In these circumstances, I consider it appropriate to retain these petitions for the present and direct the Sessions Judge, Multan, to conduct a limited inquiry into the girls’ circumstances and submit a report identifying the arrangements available for their immediate protection. The report shall assist this Court in determining the relief to be granted, without affecting the jurisdiction of the competent Family Court to adjudicate guardianship and custody.

49. Pending receipt of the Sessions Judge’s report, the competing claims to custody and the concerns regarding the girls’ safety make it necessary to maintain their present accommodation in Dar-ul-Aman for a limited period. I have considered their objections to continued residence there. However, in the absence of a satisfactory assessment of the available alternatives, their immediate release to either claimant would be premature. I accordingly direct, in exercise of this Court’s jurisdiction under Article 199(1)(b)(i) of the Constitution, that they remain in Dar-ul-Aman until the next hearing, which shall take place within seven days of pronouncement of this order. This interim arrangement shall remain subject to earlier reconsideration and shall not validate the Magistrate’s orders or determine the competing claims to custody.
50. Accordingly, it is directed as follows:

(i) The orders dated 03.09.2026, 07.09.2026, 11.09.2026 and 15.09.2026 passed by the Judicial Magistrate are set aside insofar as they direct or continue the compulsory custody of Mafia Bibi and Saleena Bibi in Dar-ul-Aman. The order dated 10.09.2026 passed by the Additional Sessions Judge is also set aside. (ii) Mafia Bibi and Saleena Bibi shall be produced before the Sessions Judge within two days of pronouncement of this order, together with the relevant record. He shall hear each girl separately, ascertain her present wishes and examine the circumstances affecting her safety. He shall also hear the persons claiming custody and may obtain assistance from Ms. Muneeza Manzoor Butt and the relevant protection authorities.

(iii) The Sessions Judge shall submit a separate report concerning each girl before the next hearing. The report shall address the available evidence regarding her age, the risks associated with the competing custodial claims and the suitability of alternative accommodation. He may recommend arrangements for her immediate protection.

(iv) The Superintendent, Dar-ul-Aman, Multan, shall ensure the girls’ safety, dignity, healthcare and access to counselling. She shall facilitate appropriate supervised communication with their families, having regard to their wishes and safety, and immediately report to this Court any circumstances requiring reconsideration of their continued accommodation.
(v) The petitions shall be listed for further hearing ten days after pronouncement of this order, whether or not the Sessions Judge’s reports have been received.
51. Nothing stated in this order shall prejudice the determination of criminal liability, the validity of the alleged marriages or the final adjudication of any claim to guardianship or custody.
